Chapter Seven: Building Essentialist Routines and Habits
Let’s talk about something that makes essentialism stick—not just for a week or two, but for the long haul.
It isn’t just about willpower. It’s about putting routines and habits in place that keep you focused, almost on autopilot. Think of habits like the rails for a train—they make sure you’re heading in the right direction, with less effort and fewer decisions along the way.
So, where do you start? The first step is to spot those key behaviors that support your most important goals. Maybe that’s setting aside a few minutes each morning to plan your day, carving out quiet time for deep work, or building in regular moments for reflection. Once you know which behaviors matter most, you can turn them into routines—these are the small, repeated actions that start to feel like second nature.
Here’s how you can build essentialist habits:
Start small—just pick one or two new habits to focus on.
Try anchoring each new habit to something you already do, like reviewing your priorities right after your morning coffee.
And don’t forget to track your progress. Celebrate those tiny wins—they’ll help you build momentum and keep going.
Remember, consistency is way more powerful than intensity. Spending just a few minutes every day on an essential habit beats trying to overhaul your whole life all at once. Over time, these little actions add up—and the results can be pretty amazing.
Routines also help guard against decision fatigue. You know that feeling when you’ve made so many choices in a day that your brain just wants to shut down? By making your key behaviors automatic, you free up mental space for the stuff that really needs your creativity and problem-solving. For example, imagine a writer who blocks off the first hour of every morning, no questions asked, just for writing. It’s non-negotiable, and it protects what matters most.
And here’s something to pay attention to—routines aren’t set in stone. Life changes, and so should your habits. It’s smart to check in now and then, see what’s working, and tweak things as you go. Essentialism is all about flexibility and learning as you move forward.
Let’s look at a real-world example. Think about a parent who wants to make family dinners a priority. By setting a routine where everyone sits down to eat together at the same time each evening, that value becomes part of daily life—not just something that gets squeezed out when things get busy.
So, what’s the key takeaway here? Building essentialist routines is about making the right choices automatic. It’s a gentle, sustainable way to make sure your actions always line up with your highest priorities.
